summary: The text of the Memorandum of Understanding signed on July 14, 1999 in Oslo by ICANN, the IETF, the ITU-T, W3C and ETSI, which creates the Protocol Support Organization within ICANN. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A signed agreement among several groups that set Internet rules, creating a shared group to advise ICANN.

subtitle: The signed agreement that created ICANN's Protocol Support Organization

tldr.problem: ICANN needed a formal, signed agreement with international standards organizations to establish how they would collectively advise ICANN on protocol matters.
tldr.mechanism: A Memorandum of Understanding signed on July 14, 1999 in Oslo by ICANN, the IETF, ITU-T, W3C, and ETSI, creating the Protocol Support Organization with a Protocol Council of representatives from each organization.
tldr.outcome: The PSO provided a framework for coordinated protocol governance from 1999 to 2004, though it was eventually superseded by other ICANN structures.

today: RFC 2691 is Informational. It documents the signed Memorandum of Understanding that created the Protocol Support Organization in 1999. The PSO operated as the formal mechanism for protocol standards input to ICANN until 2004, when it was discontinued and replaced by other advisory structures.

sections.title: Purpose and Signatories
sections.content:
This is the text of the Memorandum of Understanding signed on July 14, 1999 in Oslo. The signatories are ICANN, the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force), the ITU-T (International Telecommunication Union - Telecommunication Standardization Sector), the W3C (World Wide Web Consortium), and ETSI (European Telecommunications Standards Institute).

The MOU establishes the Protocol Support Organization (PSO), which serves as a consensus-based advisory body within ICANN's framework. It creates both a Protocol Council for formal decision-making and an annual open General Assembly for public participation.
sections.eli5: Five organizations signed an agreement in Norway creating a group that would advise ICANN about Internet protocols.

sections.title: Protocol Council Composition and Operations
sections.content:
Each signing SDO appoints two members to the Protocol Council, each serving for a term set by that SDO. The SDO can change its members at will but must notify the Protocol Council Secretary and ratify its choices at least annually. Meeting quorum requires at least a majority of members present representing at least three-quarters of the SDOs.

Unless otherwise specified in the MOU, all Protocol Council actions are taken by majority vote. The Council can meet in person with 45 days' notice or by phone with 15 days' notice. The Council maintains a web site and has a Secretary whose position rotates among the SDOs, with the IETF providing the initial Secretary.
sections.eli5: Each of the five groups picks two people to be on the Council, which votes on decisions. The Council keeps a website and meetings are public.

sections.title: ICANN Board Appointments and Advisory Role
sections.content:
The Protocol Council appoints Directors to the ICANN Board according to ICANN's By-laws. When ICANN has vacancies that the PSO can fill, ICANN notifies the Council. The Council holds an open call for nominations from the SDO signatories and the public. The PSO-nominated Directors are selected through a process the Council determines, but must meet the criterion that no more than 2 may be residents of the same geographic region.

Importantly, PSO-nominated Directors function as full ICANN Board Directors, not as PSO representatives. The Protocol Council's advisory role is limited to matters that the ICANN Board refers to it that relate to assignment of parameters for Internet protocols.
sections.eli5: The Council picks some people to sit on ICANN's board and help run it. Those people work as full board members, not just to represent the Protocol groups.

sections.title: Policy Development and Conflict Resolution
sections.content:
The MOU commits the PSO to the proposition that policies for protocol parameter assignments are the responsibility of the individual SDO that developed the protocol, following Internet tradition. The Protocol Council and ICANN are available to help SDOs develop policies and procedures for resolving conflicts between SDOs.

Crucially, any such policies and procedures must be adopted only with the agreement of all SDOs. The ICANN Board takes no additional action regarding disputes between SDOs related to protocol assignment or registration—the SDOs work things out themselves with the Council's assistance.
sections.eli5: Each standards group stays in charge of its own protocol rules. If two groups disagree about something, the Council helps them figure it out, but everyone has to agree to any solution.

sections.title: General Assembly and Public Participation
sections.content:
The Protocol Council hosts an open meeting called the General Assembly at least once per year, permitting open participation by all interested individuals. Each General Assembly is hosted by a signing SDO in conjunction with one of its major meetings, with an effort to rotate locations geographically to avoid consecutive meetings in the same region.

The schedule and agenda for the General Assembly are posted at least 90 days in advance on the PSO web site. Protocol Council meeting notices are posted at least 45 days before physical meetings or 15 days before telephonic or electronic meetings (or shorter if all SDOs agree). Minutes from all PSO meetings are publicly posted within 30 days of the meeting.
sections.eli5: Anyone can attend an open meeting once a year, and all the Council's meetings and notes are public for everyone to read.
